chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Abu al-Qasim al-Sayqal, who said:

I wrote to him: 'The scabbards of swords, which are called As-Safan, are made from fish skins; is it permissible to use them for work, given that we do not eat their flesh?' He (peace be upon him) wrote: 'There is no problem.'

key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ: there is no problem / it is permissible

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to use fish skins for sword scabbards if the fish is not eaten?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Rida (or Imam al-Jawad, depending on the specific chain context in *Al-Kafi*) clarifies that the permissibility of using fish skins for sword scabbards (*Safan*) is not contingent upon the fish being edible, thereby distinguishing between the ritual purity of the skin and the dietary laws of consumption. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle that the impurity (*najis*) of a fish's flesh does not necessarily render its skin impure if it is properly tanned or used for non-food purposes, emphasizing practical utility in material culture.

en.hubeali: Muhammad Bin Yahya, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad, from Muhammad Bin Isa, from Abu Al Qasim Al Sayqal who said,

‘I wrote to him<sup>asws</sup>, ‘The studding of the swords which are names as Al-Saffan, having been taken from the fish skins, so is it allowed to be working on it and we do not eat its flesh?’ So he<sup>asws</sup> wrote: ‘There is no problem’.
en.sarwar: 10. Muhammad ibn Yahya has narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn ‘Isa from abu al-Qasim al-Sayqal who has said the following: “

I once wrote to him (the Imam), ‘Alayhi al-Salam, and asked, ‘There is a certain sheathing of swords called al-Safan (sandpaper) which is from skin of fish; if it is permissible to work with and we do not eat its meat.’ He (the Imam) wrote back, ‘It is not unlawful.’”
